title: Groupe de Barsotti-Tate et cristaux (jusqu’en été 1969) : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: A is an abelian scheme over a base S of characteristic p, assumed ordinary on this page. The previous page built the Hasse invariant σ_A as a section of ω_A^{⊗(p-1)} and a canonical isomorphism ω_A ≅ ω_{A*} (via det DR^1). It ended by claiming that, for ordinary A, this isomorphism should induce det(_pA)_et ≅ det(_pA*)_et. This page passes from level p to the full p-adic tower.

(1) Étale Tate module. Define T_p(A)_et = lim_ν (_{p^ν}A)_et. This is the Tate module of the étale quotient of the Barsotti–Tate group A[p^∞]. It is a lisse Z_p-sheaf of rank g on S.

(2) Connected–étale filtration. Here T_p(A) must mean the projective system of finite flat group schemes _{p^ν}A, not a Galois module of points: in characteristic p the connected part has no points. In the ordinary case there is an extension
0 → T_p(A)_rad → T_p(A) → T_p(A)_et → 0.
The sub-object T_p(A)_rad ('radiciel' = infinitesimal, here of multiplicative type) is the connected part.

(3) Cartier duality. Cartier duality identifies A*[p^∞] with the dual of A[p^∞] and reverses the filtration. Hence the graded pieces are exchanged:
T_p(A)_rad ≅ D(T_p(A*)_et) and T_p(A*)_rad ≅ D(T_p(A)_et).
Here D is the Cartier dual, i.e. Hom(–, Z_p(1)), which turns a lisse Z_p-sheaf into a group of multiplicative type.

(4) Consequence. The pair (T_p(A)_et, T_p(A*)_et) determines both graded pieces of T_p(A). Over a perfect base the connected–étale sequence splits, so the pair determines T_p(A) itself. Over a general base one must still describe the extension class, an element of Ext^1(T_p(A)_et, D(T_p(A*)_et)). This is exactly what Serre–Tate local moduli / canonical coordinates do: the class q ∈ Hom(T_pA_et ⊗ T_pA*_et, Ĝ_m).

(5) Goal. The page ends by announcing a 'corresponding theorem', stated on the next page: a canonical isomorphism det T_p(A)_et ≅ det T_p(A*)_et. This would be the p-adic analogue of det T_ℓ(A) ≅ det T_ℓ(A*) ≅ Z_ℓ(g), and the étale incarnation of ω_A ≅ ω_{A*}.
- For ordinary A, Lie of the multiplicative part identifies ω_A with roughly det T_p(A*)_et ⊗ O_S, up to dualization and twist. So line bundles on the ordinary locus become rank-one p-adic characters. This is the mechanism later exploited by Katz in his p-adic modular forms and Igusa-tower work.
- On the next page Grothendieck tries to define the isomorphism via a polarization φ: α_p(φ) = det(T_p(φ)_et)/sqrt(deg φ), and must show it is independent of φ.
- The square root makes sense up to a unit: the kernel of a polarization is Cartier self-dual, so its étale and multiplicative parts have equal order. Hence the p-part of deg φ equals |det T_p(φ)_et|^{-2}.
- A lemma attempting the same for arbitrary endomorphisms is crossed out as 'faux'. Correctly so: the statement uses symmetry, which only polarizations have.
errors: T_p(A)_rad cannot be read as a Tate module of points (it would be zero in char p). The whole discussion only makes sense for the Barsotti–Tate group, i.e. the system of finite flat group schemes. The notation is slightly abusive but Grothendieck evidently means this.

'Base parfaite ⇒ T_p(A) is determined by its graded pieces' needs care. Over a perfect field the connected–étale sequence splits canonically. Over a perfect base scheme one still needs local triviality of the relevant fppf Ext (units being p-divisible); this holds étale-locally, but globally Pic-type contributions could in principle intervene. Grothendieck flags the general case himself ('il y aurait lieu d'expliciter la structure d'extension').
D must include the Tate twist (Hom(–, Z_p(1)) / Cartier dual) for the stated isomorphisms to hold. This is implicit in the notation.
Next-page issue (context): α_p is written with ⊗Q_ℓ where Q_p is meant. The square root of deg φ is only defined up to the prime-to-p part and units.

ideas.what: Étale Tate module of an ordinary abelian scheme as a lisse Z_p-sheaf; connected–étale exact sequence of the p-divisible group
ideas.modern_name: Connected–étale (multiplicative–étale) filtration of an ordinary Barsotti–Tate group
ideas.usually_credited_to: Tate (p-divisible groups, 1966), Serre–Tate, Messing; Grothendieck's Barsotti–Tate theory
ideas.where_published: Groupes de Barsotti–Tate et cristaux de Dieudonné (Montréal 1970); ICM Nice 1970 talk

ideas.what: Cartier duality exchanges the étale and multiplicative graded pieces of A[p^∞] and A*[p^∞]
ideas.modern_name: Cartier/Serre duality of p-divisible groups compatible with filtrations

ideas.what: Over a non-perfect base, the ordinary Barsotti–Tate group is an extension class of the étale part by the dual of A*'s étale part, still to be made explicit
ideas.modern_name: Serre–Tate canonical coordinates / extension class q(A)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Serre–Tate (Woods Hole 1964), Katz 'Serre–Tate local moduli' (1981), Messing (1972)

ideas.what: Desired canonical isomorphism det T_p(A)_et ≅ det T_p(A*)_et as p-adic analogue of det T_ℓ(A) ≅ det T_ℓ(A*), linked to ω_A ≅ ω_{A*} and the Hasse invariant
ideas.modern_name: Identification of the Hodge line bundle on the ordinary locus with a p-adic character (Igusa tower / p-adic modular forms)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Katz (p-adic properties of modular schemes, 1973); Igusa; Deligne–Ribet setting

missed.claim: Grothendieck seeks a canonical, polarization-independent isomorphism det T_p(A)_et ≅ det T_p(A*)_et for ordinary abelian schemes. It is meant as the étale counterpart of his canonical ω_A ≅ ω_{A*} and of the Weil-pairing determinant. The ingredients (Hasse invariant, ω, det of étale Tate module) are close to Katz's later p-adic modular forms framework, but this explicit formulation is not a standard statement in the literature.
missed.quote: donc la connaissance de T_p(A)_et et T_p(A^*)_et permet de reconstituer les deux facteurs de T_p(A) ... On aimerait aussi d'établir un théorème correspondant
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is a minor variant of known results (Katz, Serre–Tate). Probably obtainable from Lie(multiplicative part) ≅ D(T_p(A*)_et) ⊗ O_S. Its main interest is historical: Grothendieck around 1969 was linking the Hasse invariant, ω and the étale p-adic characters of the ordinary locus.

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics is standard: the connected–étale sequence, Cartier duality swapping the pieces, and the reference to Serre–Tate-type extension data. The only mildly notable point is the explicit program, spread over these pages, to match the Hasse invariant and ω_A ≅ ω_{A*} with a canonical isomorphism of determinants of étale Tate modules. This anticipates themes Katz developed in 1973 but is not a new result.
transcription_corrections: The crossed-out symbol before (_{p^ν}A)_et under lim← is an abandoned notation; the intended formula is simply T_p(A)_et = lim←_ν (_{p^ν}A)_et.
The final line is likely 'On aurait envie d'établir un théorème corres-' (or 'On aimerait aussi établir ...'); the words after 'un' are hard to read. A crossed-out word follows on the next line.
'(N.B.' opens a parenthetical that is never closed in the manuscript.
